core_obligations: Choose a component with maximal ratio (proof lines 1653-1668): for the generic point of each component the local ring is a discrete valuation ring; let e_i be the valuation of the chosen meromorphic function and d_i that of a local equation of the divisor, both nonnegative, and pick an index where the ratio is maximal; replacing the function by a suitable power and the divisor by a multiple is permissible because the associated invertible sheaf behaves accordingly and degrees are multiplied by the same factor.

Show the function vanishes on the divisor (proof lines 1668-1680): the image of the function in the structure sheaf of the divisor vanishes at the generic points of all components by the choice of the maximal index, and since the divisor satisfies (S1) it has no embedded associated points, so a section vanishing at the generic points of the components is zero.

Conclude positivity of the degree (proof lines 1680-1686): hence the function is a global section of the ideal sheaf of the divisor which generates that ideal at the chosen generic point, so its image in the sections of the conormal sheaf over that component is nonzero; by the choice of the function that image has a zero, so the degree of the conormal sheaf restricted to that component is positive, which in particular prevents the conormal sheaf from being trivial.
proof_roadmap: Normalize by replacing the divisor with a multiple chosen so that a ratio of valuations is maximal.
Use the absence of embedded associated points to show the chosen function vanishes on the divisor.
Read off that the resulting nonzero section of the conormal sheaf has a zero and hence positive degree.
difficulty_reason: The lemma proves that for a nonempty effective Cartier divisor contained set theoretically in the closed fibre of the vanishing situation, the conormal sheaf of the divisor is not trivial; more precisely some component carries a restriction of positive degree (statement lines 1643-1651). The proof (proof lines 1653-1689) normalizes the divisor by a suitable multiple so that a ratio of valuations is maximal, uses the (S1) property to show that the chosen function vanishes on the divisor, and concludes that a nonzero section of the conormal sheaf has a zero, hence positive degree. H2: a valuation-theoretic normalization with three inputs, written out in full.
